name: Website Helpers and Resource Directories
title: Website Helpers and Resource Directories
answer: A website helper is a chat tool on a district website that answers common family questions about enrollment, schedules, and services at any hour, drawing only on verified district information and admitting when it does not know. A family resource directory is a checked list of services such as food assistance, health care, and tutoring that a limited chat tool can help families search. Both matter because families need reliable answers without losing the ability to reach a person.

sections.body: Many families have questions about enrollment, schedules, and services, and a website helper can answer the common ones at any hour. The tool solves the problem of families waiting for answers outside office hours by drawing only on verified district information. It must say clearly when it does not know rather than guessing. A family resource directory addresses a related problem, helping families find services such as food assistance, health care, and tutoring. A chat tool limited to a verified list of resources can help families search that list.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, a chat tool sits on the website and answers common questions about enrollment, schedules, and services at any hour, using only verified district information. The same tool can be limited to a verified list of resources so families can search for food assistance, health care, and tutoring. Every resource on the list should be checked regularly because services change. The tool should never invent a resource that is not on the list, and it should say clearly when it does not know. Families should always be able to reach a person, with a staffed phone line and email kept available and easy to find.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It offers the Los Angeles case from Chapter 3 as a warning: the district's chatbot vendor collapsed, leaving the district without the service it had paid for. That case is presented as a cautionary example rather than research, so the idea rests on practice and experience rather than a research base.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A website helper should never be the only way families can get help. A staffed phone line and email should remain available and easy to find, so families always have a route to a person. The tool must draw only on verified district information and say clearly when it does not know. It should never invent a resource that is not on the verified list, and every resource on that list should be checked regularly since services change. The Los Angeles case shows the risk of depending on a vendor that may collapse, so the decision to keep human contact and verified information in place stays with the district.
